protections: Safe mode blocks saving a non-empty PHP code section through the CMS object model: CmsCompoundObject::beforeSave() calls checkSafeMode(), which throws when cms.enableSafeMode is on, the code attribute is dirty and trim(code) is non-empty (modules/cms/classes/CmsCompoundObject.php:99, modules/cms/classes/CmsCompoundObject.php:147).
Safe-mode editor guard: the CMS template editor marks the code field readOnly and reveals the safe-mode notice while cms.enableSafeMode is on (modules/cms/controllers/Index.php:76).

Theme-management authorization: the Themes controller is limited to cms.manage_themes/cms.manage_theme_options and a beforeDisplay listener redirects users without cms.manage_themes (modules/cms/controllers/Themes.php:31, modules/cms/controllers/Themes.php:52).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: Theme import is a trusted whole-package operation performed by a user who already holds cms.manage_themes, so imported files are treated as administrator-supplied code.
Marketplace archives are fetched from the October gateway with a hash by a user holding system.manage_updates, so their contents are vendor-trusted.
The shipped safe-mode message says only editing of the PHP code section is disabled, so code sections already deployed on disk by a developer are trusted and expected to keep executing.

Committing or syncing a stored template requires app.debug (modules/cms/controllers/Index.php:519) and the database template layer, which is off by default (config/cms.php:253), so the route looks unreachable in a hardened install.
A section separator appearing in markup is ordinary content, and splitting or escaping template sections is the Halcyon processor's responsibility (october/rain), not a CMS-controller check.

masking: T3 masks T1/T2/T4: if the shared execution layer is assumed to enforce safe mode, every write route looks harmless, and conversely blocking one write route does not stop a code section already on disk from running.

T5 can leave a stored template whose serialized content holds a code section even though the code attribute was never dirty; T4 then writes that stored content to the filesystem, so closing T1/T2 alone leaves this persistence path.
Closing T5 by validating serialized sections does not close T1, and closing T1 by rejecting imported code sections does not close T5.

conflicts.what: A blunt import validator that rejects any template containing a section separator would also reject legitimate page content; the import check and the serialization check must be content-aware and separate edits.

A CodeParser/Controller safe-mode gate (T3) would stop legitimate developer-deployed code sections and would let a solver skip per-write-route guards; enforcing safe mode at T1 instead keeps code sections executable, so the two fixes encode opposite contracts.

Gating execution (T3) makes the datasource write path (T4) harmless at runtime but it still writes the content to disk for later; gating writes (T4) leaves the execution layer open for every other producer, so a fix must decide which layer owns safe mode.

fairness_risks: The shipped safe-mode message says editing the PHP code section is disabled; a rule that refuses to execute any code section while safe mode is on contradicts that documented behaviour for developer-deployed themes.
Legitimate theme import, duplication, marketplace install and theme:sync must keep working, so safe mode cannot simply disable those features.
Markup legitimately contains separator-style lines and settings values can be multi-line; refusing that input shape breaks valid templates.
The strlen(trim(code)) branch in checkSafeMode exists so an existing code section can be cleared while safe mode is on; blocking any dirty code attribute breaks that legitimate operation.
Theme packages legitimately carry .htm, .md and .txt assets, so an extension allowlist added for the import or upload paths must not reuse the narrow editable-asset list.

design.why: T1 is the administrative route that never touches the guarded model and is the most plausible later-fix (B) site; T3 is a shared lower-layer absence whose dismissal (safe mode only blocks editing) is exactly the kind DeepSeek accepts; T5 is a how-type serialization shape a plausible check mishandles, the kind MiMo misses; T4 is a second write implementation with a debug-only dismissal. Each needs a different edit (import validation, an execution-layer policy decision, section/serialization validation, datasource write check) and each has a different reason to dismiss, so no single insight closes the set. T2 is a fifth, weaker option (trusted marketplace) if a fifth trap is wanted.

unverified: The Halcyon Processor/SectionParser source lives in the october/rain dependency and is not vendored in this worktree; T5 rests on the fixture-evidenced section-count format plus the absence of any separator validation in this repository, not on reading the serializer itself.

No Twig SandboxExtension or SecurityPolicy exists anywhere in the pinned PHP tree, so 'Twig sandbox escape' is read as the CMS safe-mode control over the PHP code section, not as Twig's own sandbox.

The default extension list used by AssetList::onUpload (FileDefinitions::get('assetExtensions'), from october/rain) is not vendored, so whether a server-executable extension can be uploaded to a theme's assets directory could not be verified; the Asset::save path does restrict to the css/js/less/sass/scss editable list (modules/cms/classes/Asset.php:250,303).

Halcyon Model::fill/setAttribute/isDirty internals are in the dependency; the analysis assumes fill() writes attributes directly, which is what makes the check inspect the model's code attribute rather than a settings mirror.
